output:
*Interview with Madame Odile Monnier, in the dining room, 1 January 1900. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, I am sorry to keep you from your rest at such an hour. I will be as brief as I can.

MME MONNIER: There is no rest in this house, Inspector. Sit down if you wish. I warn you that I am not a helpful witness at this hour.

MATTHEY: Tell me what you can, in your own order. Begin with dinner, if you like.

MME MONNIER: My husband made us show our watches, as he does every year. When the temple struck nine, he held out his hand and we each took ours from our pockets. Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. My husband told him so, in front of everyone, and said that a watch in that condition was a disgrace to the family. Félix laughed, which is what he does when he is embarrassed. He has carried that silver thing since his father died, and he will let no one touch it. Aurèle knew that. He could not resist.

MATTHEY: Was there any quarrel at the table?

MME MONNIER: Monsieur Girard and my husband quarrelled about the price of the repeater. Girard wished to buy the rights to it. My husband would not sell, and Girard would not be refused. I did not follow the figures.

MATTHEY: And afterwards?

MME MONNIER: Afterwards we were in the salon. I looked at the salon clock when the temple struck ten. It showed five minutes to ten. I remember that because I had been waiting for the temple, and it was a relief to be told something I could rely on.

MATTHEY: Who was with you in the salon?

MME MONNIER: Casimir and I sat down to piquet. We played without a break. He is the family's doctor, and he has been our friend for thirty years. He is the oldest friend this house has. He went out at twenty-eight minutes past ten by the salon clock, to fetch his cigars. As he went out he asked me to play for him.

MATTHEY: What did you do then?

MME MONNIER: I sat down at the piano at once. I play Chopin, which you may have been told, and I played it until he came back. I stopped when he came in. A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Thank you. You have been very exact.

MME MONNIER: I have been exact all my life. It is the one virtue my father left me, along with his opinions on sermons.

MATTHEY: You have been married thirty years, I believe.

MME MONNIER: Thirty years. Do not ask me whether I loved him, Inspector. I loved him for a long time, and then I loved him the way one loves a good coat, every day and without noticing. He was a difficult man. He was also the finest watchmaker in the canton, and I would not let anyone say otherwise.

MATTHEY: Félix has debts, I understand.

MME MONNIER: Félix has debts to half of Le Locle, and some of them to Girard. I told him that his debts were his own affair. I was wrong to say it so easily. Aurèle would have paid them and never let him forget it. I am not sure which of those I would have preferred for him.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you would like to add?

MME MONNIER: Only that Aurèle spent four years on that repeater. He meant to strike the new century with it. He did not want the rest of us to know how frightened he was that he would not finish. Lina could tell you the hours he spent on it. I could not. I was never allowed in the atelier.

MATTHEY: Madame, I know this is not easy.

MME MONNIER: You will want me to weep, Inspector. I will not do it in front of a policeman, and I will not do it in front of Casimir either. Write down that I did not.
